utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Colonel Doyle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We did start last week, so let's carry on and talk about what we agreed during our interview. You confirmed that you didn't know that the Serbs did not obstruct the Muslim referendum on independence. Do you accept now that it was the Serb position was this: We had our referendum. The other two communities can and should have their own referendum or plebiscite in order to see the will of the people prevail, and all this was subject to procedure for amendments to the constitution in the Assembly. Do -- are you aware of that? Do you have knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware that the Bosnian Serbs had the referendum and that the parliamentary debate on the holding of the referendum was carried by the Croats and the Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My point is this: Do you remember that the Serbs had nothing against their referendum and that they didn't obstruct it in any way and enabled it to go through on the territory where they had power and where they were the decisive majority?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, are you referring to the Serbs had nothing against -- is it their referendum or the other referendum? Could you clarify that point for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My position is this, and we shall come to that: You were at the meeting. We proposed that regionalisation be conducted first and that we go to a national referendum. As that was not successful, we had nothing against that the other two communities should carry out their own referendum and we didn't obstruct their referendum. Nowhere, there were no incidents anywhere. I'm talking about the referendum at the end of February.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm not quite clear on one thing in your report where it says very nicely and clearly what the cause of the demonstrations were in Sarajevo -- or, rather, the barricade. However, during the examination-in-chief, you mostly said that the results of the referendum were the reason, whereas in your report it says that the reason was the killing of the wedding -- in the wedding party, and then during the in chief you talked about the referendum. Now, our position is that the results of the referendum did contribute to this but not with barricades but the behaviour of those criminals that attacked the Serb wedding party. Now, do you agree with your report, what you say in your report, that the pretext or the reason was the killings that -- the killing that took place at the wedding party and that that was a major event?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report that I made out at the conclusion of the referendum debate was that the barricades were erected by the Bosnian Serbs and that there were two factors. The two factors were, one, the result of the referendum; and two, according to the Bosnian Serbs, the reason the barricades were raised was because the death -- the killing at the wedding. So I took that -- the fact that the Bosnian Serbs told me that in their view the reason why the barricades went up was the killing at the wedding. I took that in consideration, and I mentioned that in addition to the results of the referendum. The point to make here is that in my view, the barricades were erected at such a time and such a short period of time that in my view there had -- there had to be some prior consideration to these being erected. That was my professional opinion at the time, and I reflected that in my report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 611040 next, please. It's the same as 21077. On e-court, please, may we have that called up. It is Prosecution 65 ter 11040 document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And there we have the first paragraph where you put in first place the fact that the killing of the Serb at the wedding ceremony was number one and that the tensions could also be attributed to the referendum. Do you see that first and second sentence: "[In English] Tension was heightened in Sarajevo as the result of all the killing of a Serb and the wounding of another at the wedding ceremony in the city of 98 [sic] February."

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the killing was on the 1st of March, in actual fact, and the barricades were erected on 1st of March. And then you go on to say: "[In English] A degree of the tensions could be also attributed to the referendum which has had --" [Interpretation] To the referendum and so on. So it is more convincing. Well, the results of the referendum were common knowledge in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina but the killing in the barricades only existed in Sarajevo, so your assessment there was a good one. However, the Prosecution seemed to like something else more. What I want to say for the transcript, it wasn't recorded, is this: That the results held true for the whole of Bosnia, but there were no barricades anywhere, whereas the killing was only in Sarajevo and it is in Sarajevo that there were barricades, only there. So at that point, your report is fairly accurate by placing the number one point first. However, the Prosecution seemed to have liked the second point better, that the results of the referendum were the reason and pretext, which they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question is why the Colonel now decided to use the conditional that he used in the second sentence, "could," although he confirmed that with time memory fades?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can we agree over another point. You said that you saw me after that, after that first and second -- at our meeting you said that you saw me. Now, I have here my secretary's diary, and he writes that you came to see me. The entry is on the 1st of March, probably in the morning, because then in that same diary it says that at 1600 hours I, too, flew together to Belgrade together with Koljevic and Krajisnik. Now, is it possible that you might have got that muddled, that you might have seen me before the assassination?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that with spoke at the meeting last week you brought this up, and I checked over my notes, and I don't think I said in the notes of my witness statement that in actual fact I met you by name on that day. When you asserted to me last week that in fact you weren't in the city, I actually accept that. It doesn't take away from the point that the Serb leadership on that day gave me a list of demands which I handed over to Ejup Ganic. So I accept the point that you say that you weren't there. It wasn't in my original report that I may have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that it would be a good idea if we were to stay with this document for a while longer, because there we can see the Serb demands handed over to the Presidency at a Presidency session, but there's something else that has caught my attention here, and it is this: You said that they said that they would erect barricades only if the word came from me; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 2 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what it says, the last sentence the first paragraph: "[In English] It became apparent from the negotiations which followed that the armed Serbs would only consider dismantling the barricades on the directive orders of the SDS leadership, however, they expressed their gratitude to the EC Monitoring Mission." [Interpretation] So not Karadzic but the leadership; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when I put down the leadership, basically, I was referring to you as the leader of the Bosnian Serbs. And your name is mentioned, as far as I recall, on my witness statement of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but not in your report, you see. And the rest of the leadership would not have agreed that I was the leadership. I was just one member of the leadership. But let's move on. Now let's have the following page. Next page on our screens, please. There we are. This is what you say here that after an agreement had been reached in the Presidency and the Presidents unanimously accepted the Serb demands and we'll go back to them in due course: "[In English] On this information being announced, the barricades began to be dismantled." [Interpretation] Therefore, Colonel, not when I gave the word but as the result of negotiations between the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party and the Presidency in which there were two members of the Serbian Democratic Party; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D1210 called up, please. I think that this document is in evidence. Is it? Has it been admitted? Associated?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was admitted as Exhibit P924.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D1210 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we have the minutes from the 56th Presidency session of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 2nd of March:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the English version, please. Zoom into the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And present were Alija Izetbegovic; Biljana Plavsic; Franjo Boras; Ejup Ganic; the Deputy Secretary Mile Dmicic; the Prime Minister and Vice-Premier Jure Pelivan and Muhamed Cengic; the Minister and Deputy Minister Alija Delimustafic, Vitomir Zepinic, General Kukanjac, and the command of the 2nd Military District, Drago Vukosavljevic, as command of the Territorial Defence. And in the second part of the session, the president of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Democratic Party took part, Rajko Dukic. He was president of the Executive Board in actual fact, but for that purpose he became involved so that he could control the events. Now, may we have page 3 called up, please. And while we're waiting for that, let me just remind you, you said that in all the negotiations I took part. Now, do you agree that that was the demand made by our mediators or that it would be disrespectful for me not to have attended but to send a deputy of mine; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I've never seen this document before. I mean, I'm -- the report that I gave was based on the information I gained at the time. The demands of the Bosnian Serbs were handed to me, and I passed them over to Ejup Ganic. Who sat at what meeting after that I wasn't a part of, so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Ganic didn't hand them over then because here we see that Dukic handed them over at the meeting itself and that that's why he was asked to attend the meeting, to negotiate and to say under what conditions he would be able to influence the people to lift the barricades. But what I asked you beforehand, do you agree that if the mediators, Vance, Owen, and others, expected me to be present then it was the proper thing to do for me to be present and that it would be disrespectful for me to send anybody else, any deputy in my stead?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not too sure why you're bringing up Cyrus Vance. I thought we were talking about a situation which prevailed in the city on the 2nd of March. You were the leader of the Bosnian Serbs. I accept that you may not have been there on that day, so I really -- I really don't understand what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is not a problem, Colonel. It's just a question of you claiming that I participated in all the negotiations, and it seems to me that this is something that the Prosecution liked, but what I would like to ask you is: Is this a regular thing, and is it a polite thing for me to respect the mediators, to attend or not? Was I expected to be present?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any time that there were negotiations held in the city of Sarajevo that I was involved in you were always present. What may have happened with people like Cyrus Vance, I simply don't know, but I'm referring to the occasions where there were negotiations being held. The Bosnian Serbs, on all occasions that I attended, was headed by yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We haven't achieved what I wanted to achieve for you to say whether this is just customary, that -- was I expected to be there, but let us look at page 2. We have page 2 in the Serbian. Can we look at page 2 in the English as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we may have to see page 1 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can see on page 2 that Rajko Dukic participated. Can we look at page 3 now, please. In the English this would be on page 2. Thank you. I am going to summarise it. The president of the Crisis Staff of the SDS, Rajko Dukic, departing from the actual situation in Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina came out with the following demands and these are the demands that you are talking about and that you have to cease all further activity, more specifically the campaign that is being waged with a goal to declare a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and to secure it's international recognition until a satisfactory and final solution is released. I hope that the English -- the interpreters have the English version in front of them. All right. Very well. And then it continues: "To unconditionally cease the campaign that is being waged in the sphere of public information supporting a sovereign and independent Bosnia." And then the next sentence: "To ensure unbiased information until the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina which is being led under the umbrella of the European community is concluded." And it goes on that the tragedy in all the places is a direct consequence of the situation in the MUP and that personnel transformation of the B and H MUP should be carried out pursuant to the agreement reached by the three leading political parties immediately after the republican elections. I'm going to ask you if you knew, Colonel, sir, that the Muslim side, as you can see, for the whole year, 13, 14 months, sabotaged the appointment of Serbian cadre to the posts in the police?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is one of the features when you live under the Muslims and not with the Muslims. You would grant -- be granted positions in the police, but they would not actually appoint those people. This is something that you should know. Perhaps it's our fault as well, but this is an important thing, and I can see that that is here, and I wonder that nobody asked themselves what this particular point meant. Did you ask yourself what this meant?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. My job on that occasion was to get the demands that were made by the Bosnian Serbs and pass them over to the Crisis Committee of the Presidency for them to come up with whether or not they would agree to accept those demands. In other words, I was a facilitator. My job was not to interpret what was being said here. My job was simply to pass on the message and try to make some progress that all sides would agree on. That was the main mission of the European Union and that's the mission I stood by; in other words, not to take sides but to pass on information, and to try and ensure that we would facilitate an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph: "To arrest the persons of the heinous crime in front of the Serbian Orthodox church in was Carsija in Sarajevo during the day." Did you know that in April the killer of the Serbian best man, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, appeared on state television in Sarajevo and boasted of having killed the best man because he had seen in the wedding party a Serbian flag? This was already when you were there, after the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm certainly not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this was insulting and humiliating for the Serbs and also irritating?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, how is the witness expected to answer that question which is both speculative and asked about an event that he didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness can answer the question, he can deal with it; otherwise he can say that he cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm accepting that because one of the conditions or one of the conditions laid down by the Bosnian Serbs was to the effect that they wanted the perpetrators of this crime arrested, I accepted that as one of the conditions. I assume it wasn't being denied by anybody, and therefore I would have accepted for what it was. But other than that I would not have a comment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that that criminal, the killer, was liquidated after the war in some cafe without having being brought to trial or having been convicted for this crime?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name had been mentioned to me before. I had been informed that he was a criminal. As to what happened to him afterwards, I had no idea. I did hear he was killed, but I didn't know any of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was the assistant commander in the 9th Mountain Brigade throughout the whole wartime period in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph is -- states: "Considering the fact that the Serbian people have been experiencing a length informational blockade and pressure to conduct and urgent division of the television and radio as well as to stop a broadcasting Jutel until the talks about the constitutional arrangement of BiH are over." And item 6: "To immediately disband the Crisis Staff of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina led by Ejup Ganic as an unconstitutional body and to urgently disarm paramilitary formations of the Green Berets which are acting openly in Sarajevo and protecting, among others, criminals-perpetrators of crimes." Colonel, sir, do you know that it was the Muslims who formed the Crisis Staffs in the Presidency first and throughout Bosnia and then the Serbs followed before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I was aware that there was a Crisis Committee of the Presidency. Who constituted that Crisis Committee, I simply don't know. The only person I met in relation to that was Ejup Ganic. So I had no knowledge as to who else was in that committee. Again I must say that my job was to pass over the demands, for they to be considered by the Presidency, by the Crisis Committee of the Presidency, and if they were acceded to, then we solved the immediate problem in the city, and that was my prime objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not holding it against you if you didn't know, and if you didn't it's more of our fault than anybody else's, but would I like to remind you that the Crisis Staff in the Presidency as an unconstitutional act, which the Presidency agreed on was used to bypass Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic as representatives of the Serbs with veto power on important Presidency decisions; thus that is one of the manifestations of life under the Muslims and not with the Muslims. Would you agree that such a Crisis Staff formed as early as September 1991 before the Serbs formed their Crisis Staffs, that it is an improper act?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't know which Crisis Committee was established first. It wasn't something that came to my attention. And not knowing that, it wasn't of any great concern to me. Once again, I have to say that any time we made approaches to any of the political parties it was a view to getting a common agreement amongst them to stop a conflict. That was our prime objective, nothing other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. And when did you come to Sarajevo for the first time? Was it early October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to Sarajevo to take over as head of the mission towards the end of November 1991. Before that I was working as a monitor in the city of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there a Crisis Staff of the Serbian Democratic Party in existence when you came and did the staff get in touch with you, communicate with you? Did it exist at all?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea as to when the Crisis Committee of the Bosnian Serbs was established. As you may recall yourself, my first official meeting with you was in February 1992, and that meeting was set up at my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please look at the next page in the Serbian and the English page can stay for now. And we can see that it states here: "An agreement was reached --" It's at the bottom of the English copy: "An agreement was reached that abolishing the barricades ends the need for the existence of the Crisis Staff of the Presidency of the SRBiH which was formed on the 21st of September, 1991." It was agreed at the same time that at the next Presidency meeting the report on the work of the Crisis Staff should be reviewed. The Crisis Staff was thus formed on the 21st of September, without any barricades, without any need as an unconstitutional act whereby the Muslim part of the Presidency conducted Presidency business without participation of the Serbian representatives, and agreement was reached here for that Crisis Staff to be abolished. Do you agree that that is what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see from the document that is in front of me, from the English translation, it says that. When there's reference to the establishment of the Crisis Committee in September 1991, I wasn't in Bosnia in September 1991. I didn't go there until October. So I wouldn't have been aware as to when this Crisis Committee was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let us look at this paragraph: "The Presidency's announcing that the referendum that has just taken place does not determine the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is the topic of the talks regarding the future organisation of BiH which are being led by the European Community. These talks should be continued urgently and their results have to respect the interests of all three nations as well as other citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This sounds good, doesn't it? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as I said, I haven't seen the detail of this document before, but I don't see any great difference between the content of this document and the content of the measures that were mentioned in my report. So we're probably repeating what's already been said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, there is no difference, but it's a little bit more complete here. There are a few things that indicate how the Presidency took into account natural, normal, legitimate demands only after the barricades, and my question is: Wouldn't it have been normal for this never to have been put on the agenda and had the barricades not been put up, the Presidency would have functioned according to the constitution. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a question I actually -- I can't answer myself, but I am finding it strange that we have now in front of us a detailed document about a Crisis Committee which is talking about the future constitution of Bosnia, yet these barricades, in your mind, were erected because of a killing at a wedding. I find it very strange that if these barricades were simply erected as a direct result of shooting at a wedding, that all of these details constitutional issues would have been discussed in order for the barricades to be taken down. So this would lead me to -- to believe that the reason the barricades went up in the front -- in the first was not, in fact, the killing at the wedding but the issue of the referendum, but that's only my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Colonel, sir, would you agree that there were considerable tensions which resulted in the killing of the best man and that the killing of the best man is the result of the tensions, not the cause of the tension? The killing is the cause of the eruption and the barricades, but the actual killing is the result, is the fruit of long-term tensions, political gainsmanship which the Muslim leadership conducted against the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't actually agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that there was an idyllic political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the killing?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm simply trying to say is that there were three different political parties in Bosnia and they could not get along with each other. And this was the indirect result of -- or this resulted in an extremely high degree of tension where everybody in the international community was aware that if these tensions continued to fester because of whatever was find them, then it would let to conflict, and our objective as to try and avoid that at all costs, and all our efforts were directed to that end. Who did what and where it was done, I don't have all the details because my appointment was head of the monitor mission, and our -- our freedom of movement and our safety and security was no longer guaranteed. Therefore, it was extremely difficult for us to get movement, to get information, and therefore we were not as effective as we might otherwise have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These are the minutes from a Presidency session, so I do understand that you did not have insight into them before that, but here you can see exactly what happened at the session in detail, and I can conclude, and may we have the last page for me to carry on, that all these conclusions were adopted unanimously, by which the Presidency confirmed that these were the legitimate goals -- or, rather, legitimate demands and that they were acceptable and accepted unanimously. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if those documents were signed, yes, I would agree. I'm looking at the document in front of me. If it has been signed by the various members, then I have to accept it. I don't have a problem with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have to read out a paragraph which we don't have in translation but we do have in Serbian. It says it was concluded that the public should be informed about this straight away and that the vice premier, Muhamed Cengic, and the president of the Crisis Staff of the SDS BiH, Rajko Dukic, after addressing the public on television should do what they can to disband the barricades from the main roads in Sarajevo. So you see there that the special involvement of these two people, Muslims and Serbs, for the barricades to be disbanded, because if you remember, there were both Muslim and Serb barricades erected; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no evidence that there were Muslim barricades in the city on that particular day. The Muslim barricades, as far as I recall, were erected maybe the day after or two days later when there was great fear that Mr. Arkan was coming to the city, because I received a message that Mr. Arkan wanted to meet me. And all of the barricades that I saw in Sarajevo on the day of the 1st, 2nd of March were manned by Bosnian Serbs, and that evening I had to negotiate my way from the Holiday Inn Hotel all the way to the airport. I had to negotiate my way through eight armed barricades which were erected and manned by Bosnian Serbs. I did not come across any Muslim check-points at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see that they did exist on the basis of other documents but may I have 1D1236 next, please. And I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you would like this document to be fully translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And there's also one issue that I'm a bit puzzled about. It claims to be the minutes of the 56th session, but when you look at the B/C/S version it doesn't look to me like minutes but rather like a report from another source summarising particular parts of something. Therefore, I would rather suggest to first mark it for identification until we have checked whether it is really what this says to be. We would like to check whether these are indeed the minutes of the 56th session of the Presidency or, rather, a filtered document published in whatever source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, can you help us in regards to this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly, yes. This was published by the national security and the future, prepared by Mr. Simic, published in 2006, that documents of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1991 to 1994, Tomo Simic prepared this. We asked the Prosecution to provide us with all the records, all the transcripts and minutes of the BH Presidency sessions, but we did not receive them. So this is what we managed to find. Tomo Simic is the editor, and I think it has already been used in one of the trials. So this is the only document that we could access, that we could come by. Now, if the Prosecution could provide us, and that would be very necessary, the entire documents of Presidency, BH Presidency, sessions, we'd be grateful. Perhaps something has been left out here, but it's the only document that we were able to find with a well-known publisher and everything else. And it is the minutes. It's not the transcript, it's the minutes, and the minutes are always a little shorter; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow who this Mr. Simic is, in what capacity he prepared this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is an associate of this institute, obviously the national security and -- for national security and the future as it's called, and he worked with the documents and prepared them on that basis. And it hasn't been challenged. Nobody's challenged it yet. He compiled a collection of documents relating to the BH Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you accept his explanation, or would you like him to call foundation witnesses to this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't think there is a need to call a witness, another witness, for this, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that be MFI D214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we kindly request that the Prosecution provides us with any documents they have linked to the BH Presidency, to disclose them to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, we have here parts, excerpts from a diary by my chef de cabinet, and it says Sunday, the 1st and 2nd, 1992. May we leaf through it further and move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1236. Yes. The diary has been admitted into evidence as 1D1236.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under number 2 it says: "Trip to Belgrade at 1600 hours." Then under 3, the Turkish ambassador, et cetera, et cetera, will come on Monday, and so on. But there's a mistake in the date. You see the SA043963 number up there at the top. Can we go back a bit through the agenda, turn back the pages? Or, rather, let's go to the next page, the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe I can be of assistance. This document is in e-court twice. Once it is the single page, and then there are several more pages under 1D01255. That's the same item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I apologise. May I have 1D1255 then, please. And there are several pages there. The date is -- well, February doesn't have 31 days. Well, let's look at SA043987, that page number, which I believe is the next page. No, 3938 are the last digits. Saturday is the 1st of February. Sunday is the 2nd of February. May we go on to the next page, please. It says Monday, the 3rd of February. And now we can move on to the 29th of February. This is Saturday, the 29th of February. And it says: "In the night between Friday and Saturday, a conflict broke out between the Serbs and Muslims at Turbe. A Serb was seriously wounded, and two Muslims killed. The Serbs erected barricades at the entrance to their village. "2. Dr. Karadzic in Banja Luka attending talks." "3. The German television programme," et cetera. May we move on to the next page, please. Sunday, the 1st of February where it should be the 1st of March. Number 1: "Three members of the European parliament mission wish to meet Dr. Karadzic," et cetera. Second, the trip to Belgrade at 1600 hours. Three, the Turkish ambassador, Omer, et cetera. May we move on to the next page, and the number on this page was 3963. Now we go on to 3964. Monday, the 2nd of March. He corrected the date himself there. It says: "Demonstrations and barricades in Sarajevo. The reason being -- or the pretext for that, the killing of a member of the Serb wedding party at Bascarsija." So he says that that was the pretext. Next. Here it says Pristina, Sarajevo, et cetera, but Wednesday the 4th of March, demonstrations in Sarajevo, situation critical, Green Berets attempted to attacked the Serb territorials. Dr. Karadzic was on Jutel with Alija Izetbegovic. So it was only on the 4th of March that I was in Sarajevo, and I appeared on television, Jutel television, with Mr. Izetbegovic for us to make a joint statement and calm the situation down. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. If Your Honour would permit me, I have a diary here which I've used before. It's -- it's very basic, but it just gives me recollection of who I may have met and when I met them on dates. Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I accept, Dr. Karadzic, when you say there was a meeting on television. I was aware of that on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. We will wait for -- to see your notes. That would be a good idea. If we could have a look at your diary entries.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My diary entry for the 3rd of March says that I was at the Presidency and I was given details of the arrangement that was made or the deal that was made. It also mentions that there were barricades erected by the Muslims and that they were very afraid, that there were rumours of - what I wrote down here - was according to them, of Chetniks arriving in the city and Mr. Arkan. And my diary for the 4th of March says that the barricades came down, situation quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That really does show that your diary and entries are very valuable. So I'll have to see with the Registrar how we can be provided them. Now, this diary by Ljubo Grkovic, I'd like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a problem with this diary because as we can see, there are obviously problems with dates provided, and we don't know who that person is. Perhaps if we get a bit more information on that person. Otherwise, I would oppose it, and the witness should be brought who made this diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Karadzic could help us as regards this diary. Who is Mr. Grkovic is and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grkovic was a journalist in the newspaper "Oslobodjenje" before the war. And just before the war broke out, he was my chef de cabinet in the Serbian Democratic Party. I was working at my clinic as a psychiatrist right up until the 1st of March and -- well, I worked in the clinic in the afternoon, and this diary was found by the investigators of the Tribunal -- or, rather, the OTP. I didn't even know it existed. And we can see looking at the number of pages, and the page numbers SA04379, et cetera, you can see the order. So there was a mistake for the 1st and 2nd of March. He made a mistake in recording the date. But if you look at the sequence, then you can see that that's it because you see the 1st of February was Saturday, the 2nd of February was Sunday, and then he continued to the 1st day of March, he wrote down February instead of writing March. So it's a document which we received through the IDS and it was obviously accessed and found by the Prosecution -- or, rather, the investigators. No, we received it from the Prosecution in one of the batches they provided us with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can confirm this -- this diary was seized by -- by the Bosnian authorities and provided to us, and now that I know who that person is, I have no objection any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit it, but mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D215.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the excerpts we just had we have a translation of, and I am informed by Mr. Reid that we do have indeed the full translation of this document, so we can provide it to e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with that explanation, you have no objection --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it will be admitted then, Exhibit D215.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence kindly requests to be provided with that translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 65 ter 6608, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been admitted as Exhibit P938.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes. And it's the minutes from the deputy's club of the Serbian Democratic Party. But I see that Mr. Kalinic was there as well. So, in fact -- well, all those Serbs who joined the Assembly of the Serbian people. May we turn to page 2 of the document, which is 090 -- ah. The English page number is 13. Page 13 for the English -- or, rather, 13, page 13 for the English. 19 and 20 for the Serbian. So page 13 for the English, please. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to what Velibor Ostojic is saying, Colonel, Velibor Ostojic whom you met for minister for information in the Bosnian government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to be reading that in the Serbian and you have it in English, Velibor Ostojic. "Gentlemen, I will merely provide some information which will really be important for taking position on some issues. "First, let me inform you that an informal body has introduced a special unit into the RTVSA, Sarajevo radio and television building without the knowledge of the government and the Ministry of Information. This can be done only in a state of emergency and under wartime conditions. I wrote a letter to the chief of the monitoring mission, Mr. Doyle. I met with him yesterday and gave him detailed information, and he promised that he would investigate this case. The man was simply flabbergasted when he heard about this event. "I asked Mr. Zepinic, Mandic, Kic, and Zuban, our entire structure in the MUP from the republic down to the municipality if they were aware of that. Nobody was. This was done when the RTSA leadership was in Banja Luka." Now, you were informed by the minister, the late minister now, regrettably, that somebody had usurped the minister's authority and placed a special unit in the TV building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct, Mr. Karadzic. I never received any letter from Mr. Ostojic. I agree with you that I had a meeting with him, and I can give the details of that meeting because I remember it quite well, but Mr. Ostojic certainly did not send me any letter. I certainly didn't receive any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he was objecting to the occupation of the television by some special forces which were there illegally?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic certainly did not mention that to me. Mr. Ostojic's primary purpose in asking to meet me was, one, to let me know that it was his view that as minister for information he should have control of the television at Sarajevo and not the Ministry of the Interior. He then went on to inform me that he had been attacked and beaten up outside his apartment and that he suspected it was done by officials from the Ministry of the Interior. I told him that it was not appropriate for me as head of the monitor mission to get involved in internal wranglings between ministries of the government, but that if I was going to do anything about it, I would first need to hear what the other side said, which was the Ministry of the Interior. I subsequently had a meeting with Mr. Hebib, who I understand was the deputy minister of the interior, who told me that under no circumstances would television come under the control of the minister for information and that the reason why he understood that Mr. Ostojic had been attacked was nothing to do with the television. It was a private matter. But at no stage did Mr. Ostojic mention to me about any special unit that had been deployed into the television Sarajevo. I have absolutely no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, this was not a private quarrel as it was informed in an insulting way. It was actually -- actually a murder attempt, and that is why we all received protection. We received protection from the regular police, including myself. But we're going to come to that when we start dealing with the transcript from your examination-in-chief. Can we tender this document. Ah, it's already been admitted. Can we look at 1D1128 now, please, to see what the command of the 2nd Military District -- actually, at the time it was probably the 4th still. No, actually, the 2nd Military District reporting to the -- report from the 17th Partisan Brigade about their area of responsibility. This is document 1D1128. We can see here that this is a military secret in perpetuity, meaning that this information is not to be revealed. Can we look at page 2. Thank you. It says here: "In the TV Sarajevo building, there is major dissatisfaction among a large number of journalists because of the constant presence of armed paramilitary formations which are present in the television building and are mingling with reporters from various towns. That is why the reports are one-sided and tendentious, and they are being written under threat of weapons. We would like you to inform your entire unit with this information." The document is dated the 23rd of April, 1992. Can we go back to page 1 now, please. You were there on the 23rd of April, weren't you? Did you know that the Sarajevo Television was full of paramilitary formation forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 1 it says: "On the 17th, 18th April 1992, the Green Berets and special forces of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried out an attack on the Pretis factory in Vogosca when five of the attackers were killed, 20 wounded and 9 captured. Seven trucks were driven away, two of them with ammunition. One hundred Golf vehicles were stolen, which are being used by the Green Berets. With a timely intervention by the JNA unit, catastrophe of broader scope was prevented." Were you aware of this attack by the paramilitary forces and the Muslim part of the joint MUP on a factory which belongs to the JNA and the ministry is being informed about it.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph states: "On the 18th to 19th April 1992, in the organisation of the Green Berets, the military industry Igman at Konjic, near Konjic, was captured, blocked. The phones were switched off in order to prevent reactions via the military." Were you aware of this action?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the next but one paragraph: "The situation in Visegrad is calming down and a key influence on this was played by units of the 2nd Military District. Several hundred of refugees were protected, primarily of Muslim ethnicity. A lot of assistance in food was given. The escalating conflict between Serbs and Muslims has led to the HOS units to strike both sides in order for the conflict to continue." This is the latest that is happening in Sarajevo. They are using shattering cannon blasts in order to increase tensions and fear among the citizens because in that way the sound effect and the explosions are magnified several times over. Sir, do you know what HOS is?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, HOS to me is one of the paramilitary organisations. We referred to all of those armed paramilitaries that were not JNA. Our collective title for them was simply paramilitaries, because there were so many types, colours, uniforms, it was very difficult to distinguish. I should say here if I may, Your Honour, that during this period Sarajevo was practically a city under siege. I was in the city of Sarajevo as the representative of Lord Carrington. I had the support of the monitor mission, but I had nobody under my command, nobody under my control. I was on my own. It was not appropriate for me, nor was it safe for me to travel around the city to investigate any of these allegations that may have been made. The city at this stage was in turmoil. It was very difficult to get an accurate reflection or a picture for what was going on. Out freedom of movement was interfered with, our safety and security was in jeopardy, so I am not at this stage able to give any detailed information about any of these incidents that are being brought up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but I believe that you know whose formation HOS is. Here it says that HOS was striking at the Muslims and at the Serbs in an attempt to escalate the conflict and that they were firing cannon in order to increase the effect. Shells were falling, among them HOS shells, both on the Serbs and on the Muslims. This is a secret document meant to remain that. So, please, do you know whose paramilitary formation HOS is?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the points that I want to raise here is that it was not a matter for me to try and identify military units, armed or otherwise, because my experience in peacekeeping led me to believe that I must maintain an impartial and neutral stance and this is something I always did, and if I was to be start writing reports about various paramilitary organisations one side or the other might indicate that somehow I was somebody's agent. So I did not get involved in the details of all of these paramilitary organisations at all. I was there as Carrington's personal representative. I was there in a diplomatic role, and I confined it to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we've heard now on several occasions the witness very clearly set out the parameters of his duties and the opportunities which he had and didn't have. It seems to me it's very necessary now for you to concentrate on questioning him about matters which it's apparent he did have actual personal knowledge. First of all, the witness will be able to assist the Tribunal a great deal easier, and secondly, we'll go a great deal faster.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency, but it's a fact that the Colonel has said a lot of things during the examination-in-chief, among them that many documents were also being admitted through him which testify to that time. So it should then be possible for me to probe the documents that I agreed to be admitted. So I would just like him to answer whether he knew -- whether he knows whose formation the HOS was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whose formation the HOS was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about the attack on the television. You affirmed or confirmed that you didn't know that the Green Berets had occupied the television building and that the -- how the news should look was being dictated. Do you then believe that the television building should and -- not and must not be a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already mentioned that I had no knowledge that the Green Berets had a unit in television. I had no proof that it was there either. So it wasn't part of my consideration. This is the first I've heard of it. It was never brought to my attention by anybody on either side that there was a unit on Sarajevo Television. You make reference to a letter I'm supposed to have received from Mr. Ostojic, which I'm telling you I did not receive. So I have no idea what you're talking about in relation to any unit going into television. And if that's the case then, any views I had of the television would not have taken into consideration the allegation that there were Green Berets there. I can talk about the attack on the television which is a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was: Do you consider or do you believe that television cannot be a legitimate target? We can just leave the presence of the military forces aside for a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's actually a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide whether anything is a legitimate military target or not, definitely not for the witness in his capacity as he was in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree with you, but when the colonel will be able to answer the question in the capacity as a military as far as he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I certainly would not deem that a television would be a target for any sort of military action. If some -- if somebody or organisation is attempting to upset or destroy the institutions of a state, then an attack on its television or on its communication complex would be one of those targets. So I don't know in what context Dr. Karadzic you're asking me this question. Can you explain it a bit clearer for me, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to say that NATO would get upset with you because you described the attack on Television Belgrade where there was no military presence, whereas here there was a military presence, and then later like you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No speech, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document. This is a confidential report to the command of the 17th Partisan Brigade. Actually, to the command of the 2nd Military District from one of the units out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object against it. First of all, we don't have a translation, and secondly, we do not really have a foundation for this document. The witness could not deal with it, and the commander Partisan -- 17th Partisan Brigade is definitely not a JNA unit. So the value and the reliability of this document has not been established. We would need to really get a foundation for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition, the witness has no knowledge about the content of this document except for the name of one of the paramilitaries, and there are no circumstances in which we need this document to assist the credibility. So as such, we will not admit it, Mr. Karadzic. And I take it it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just be given a minute to say that the Defence is -- well, would like to say that this is an attack on the television, and it shows that the television station building was a military facility and this is the JNA right up until the 20th of May. So the Defence is disappointed. And we certainly shouldn't -- wouldn't have called it the Partisan Brigade, because we were against the partisans and Chetniks for a modern Serb society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have ample opportunity to lead that evidence later on. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic, bearing in mind what Judge Morrison had told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before we resume the cross-examination, I wanted to ask if the Chamber might be willing to entertain a request that we have concerning the agenda of Colonel Doyle, and our request is that he go and at some point convenient to him today make a photocopy of those pages of his agenda which deal with the issues that have been the subject of his testimony, either meetings or events, and redact from those pages any personal information that he doesn't want to share with us and then have that made available to us before Dr. Karadzic concludes his cross-examination in the event that any material arising from those notes can be useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, in fact, we leave it in the hands of the parties and witnesses negotiation, but can I ask, Colonel Doyle, what your position is as to the request from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is a very personal diary to me, and it contains written notes in relation to communications I've had with my family over that period. The diary basically was made out just to remind me of who I met and where I met. The diaries don't have any personal notes as to views or opinions or reports. So -- so my request would be that I will do, of course, what I'm told to do, and if any of this was to be photocopied, I would reserve the right to delete most of its content because it is personal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It may be slightly more time-consuming, but if you were going to have to go through a photocopy it would take time anyway. It might be simply better for you to make a separate annotation on a separate piece of paper of those meetings which are relevant and the people there. And that sort of information may be easier for you and it may be more productive for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think, Your Honours, the area of the diary which -- which -- in which I had notations on who I met probably would be from the period of the 1st of March to the day I was evacuated on the 12th of May. Now, I don't have any problems to having those dates if the Defence wish having those photocopied, but I would reserve the right just to delete anything that's personal. I really don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's very kind, but normally the position is where a diary is referred to in court then it becomes a matter which can be disclosed to the Defence. For instance, if a police officer is giving evidence from his notebook, the same principle applies whether it's called a notebook or a diary, but the same principle of nondisclosure also applies in that those parts of the notebook which are not relevant to the case are not disclosed, and in your case it would be those parts personal to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- I don't have a problem with that. But as I said, it -- you know, to do it for the entire period of the full year, I think, is not necessary. I would suggest from the period of the 1st of March when the situation began to develop to the period that I was evacuated on the 12th of May. I don't have a problem with that if Your Honours so wish what to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We do appreciate your co-operation. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, may I have 1D01273 next, please. Let's just identify the first page and then we can move on to page 4 of this document. And that portion has been translated as well. So there we have the first page of the document. Now page 4 of the Serbian and -- well, it's been translated in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, here we see a report from the police of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the national security department -- or, rather, the secret service, and it says Ilidza. And they are reporting and saying that Television Sarajevo has been taken over by the Green Berets, that there are 50 to 70 of them led by Sejo Saric, and then a man called Boca and another man called Saban, with assistance from Bajrovic and Kasim, and so on, and that they have large quantities of ammunition, and during the attack on Svrakino Selo, 30 to 40 members of the Green Berets had arrived at the television station, put up launchers and bazookas on top of the TV station and that they fired at ranges of 500 metres and also present -- well, were TV station employees begged the Green Berets to provide them with ammunition so that they could exchange it in the city for bread, exchange ammunition for bread. And then it goes on to say that when it was bombed on the 9th of May, and when the 6th floor was precisely hit, the result was the destruction of studio 1 and offices and the 7th floor was hit, and so on and so forth. Now, is this proof and evidence that the building was indeed used as primarily a military facility, target?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. As far as I'm concerned, I never saw any military units at the Sarajevo Television. There was never any reference to me. Nobody from the Bosnian Serbs came to me to say anything about this. This is all absolutely astonishing for me to read. I find this very difficult to believe or accept. I never saw, during the period that I was in Sarajevo, any large military units at the television. I never saw any weapons placed on the -- on the roofs, and considering that there was a mortar attack done by the Bosnian Serbs on the television station, I'm just wondering is this ammunition to, in some way, justify the attack. But I have to say that for the period that I was there, I never saw any Green Berets or anybody in uniform or any large quantity of weapons or anything of that nature, and nobody every said a word to me from any side about this allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel, we have to clarify some things that are contradictory. You said that you were alone and helpless and that you had no other people. When we talked, you said that you didn't go into the centre of town but that you did have your people in the centre of town. Now, let's see, were you in a position to see something, and if you didn't see something, do you allow for the possibility that it happened and existed regardless of the fact that you didn't see?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just clarify the position here. Up until the time that I became the personal representative of Lord Carrington, I had control over approximately 60 monitors of the European Union that were under my command in the city of Sarajevo and throughout the country. They were tasked by me to submit daily reports on developments in their various areas. This would have included the city of Sarajevo. When I became Lord Carrington's personal representative and I returned to Sarajevo on the 10th of April, 1992, while I did have the support of the monitor mission and was able to get reports from them, I didn't have any control or authority over them. The second thing I would point out is that the Television Sarajevo was relatively close to where we were staying in Ilidza. It's not -- Sarajevo Television was not in the centre of the city. Therefore we knew and were able to have contact with Sarajevo Television. I did many interviews from Sarajevo Television. So I can only give you my personal opinion that in my mind this whole report alleging that there were bazookas and all sorts of munitions, I just can't accept that. That is my opinion and assessment at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, were you in a position to know more than state security? Because this is a document dated the 11th of May. So you claim to know better than the state security and you are also saying that this isn't an authentic document. You were alone in Ilidza and this is state security with branches everywhere, like any intelligence services, and now you're claiming you have better insight into the situation and you're challenging an authentic document from that time, a contemporaneous document. Is that what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's a complete misrepresentation. What the witness said was what he saw and what he personally didn't see, which is of course what any witness is limited to saying. He doubts the authenticity of the document on the basis of what he saw. The authenticity of the document per se is not something that this witness can speak to. If you have evidence in due course that authenticates the document, then you're free to bring it, but you've misrepresented entirely the nature and substance of the witness's evidence on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, my dilemma is in the following: You talk about many things. During the examination-in-chief you talked about many things. Now, when I went to ask you about the details of those events or things, you say you don't know, or you claim that you know differently from what the documents show. So are you biased, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the one thing I will never be accused of, Mr. Karadzic, is being biased, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me ask you, why did you avoid seeing the Serb side, meeting with the Serb side or having your photograph taken with the Serb side? Wasn't the Serb side an equal party in the negotiations and in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- is there a question there about meeting the Serbs? Does it relate to a particular time and incident? I am not sure I understand the question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is: When you were in the European mission, and I see later on, too, you refused to be a guest at Ilidza with the local leadership there, and when you came to Pale, your condition was -- that you stipulated was that you shouldn't be photographed for television. Now, I'm wondering why all the high representatives respected all three sides, whereas you were against having anything to do with the Serb side? So that's the question.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I can -- I can answer that. The first instance you are referring to is a dinner that I was invited to by a newly formed Bosnian Serb community committee in Ilidza. At that dinner I began to realise that I was being used, I would say, in a political manner. The entire non-Serb members of the hotel staff had been taken by the Bosnian Serbs and removed without their consent into the centre of the city. My view at the time when this speech was made in my presence was that they wanted to welcome me, and I felt that if I was to be seen to be part of this new organisation, it would somehow give legitimacy to it. This is something I was not prepared to do. In reference to the meeting in Pale in which I went up with Mrs. Plavsic. Mrs. Plavsic agreed with me that there would not be any publicity of my visit, because at that stage the entity of Bosnia Srpska had not been accepted internationally. And again if I was seen up in Pale in uniform of the European Union Monitor Mission and publicity was given, it somehow might be interpreted as an acceptance of the entity of Republika Srpska, and this is something I wanted to avoid because I was trying to maintain my neutrality and impartiality. As events turned out, because Mrs. Plavsic realised it was my birthday, she arranged for a cake to be brought in and the televisions arrived and photographed and covered all this, and of course, it was given prominence, I understand, even in one of the papers in Belgrade. So you have to appreciate that what I've been trying to do is I've been trying to maintain a neutral stance and that's the reason why I didn't want any publicity. I never at any stage refused to mediate or co-operate with the Bosnian Serb leadership. I think you will have to accept that yourself, Mr. Karadzic. I never refused any meeting, and I tried to be as helpful as I could to all sides in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I now tender this document, Your Excellencies. And I should like to call up 1D1291 next, please, briefly. It's a book by General MacKenzie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to ID 1273, the same opposition applies like with the previous document. It was not adopted by the witness. The witness could not deal with it at all. There's no foundation to accept this document at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed. We'll not admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're disappointed again, because it shows that the witness was not sufficiently well informed about matters, but it's your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to draw your attention to this next document. That's the title page of General MacKenzie's book. And now may we turn to page 182 of the book, please. Page 182. 182. That's what it says on the page. It's page 182 of the book. Or, rather, page 22 if we look at the document itself. Yes, that's right. Let's see what General MacKenzie has to say: "[In English] May 11th. The European Community had been conducting marathon peace talks over the previous few days. The EC continued to exclude the Bosnian Serbs from the deliberations, and as a result, was becoming less and less popular with them. Meanwhile, the Bosnian Serbs under Dr. Karadzic were becoming more and more independent from the JNA. There were even reports of Bosnian Serbs attacking JNA," and so on. [Interpretation] So you see, that that was the position taken by General MacKenzie, too, that the European Commission -- or European Community, rather, that its representatives bypassed us. Now, the position of the entire conference, including Carrington, and you accepted that when we had our interview that it was his position, Carrington's position, that the only important thing was for all three sides to place their signature to the peace agreement and everybody treat us as equal parties in the negotiations and in the conflict later on, except for the European mission. And now at the bottom of that page under May the 12th, it says: "[In English] After a restless night in new surroundings, I sat around with General Nambiar, Philippe Morillon, and Cedric Thornberry to discuss our expanding peacekeeping role in Bosnia. We still didn't have a mandate from the UN for Bosnia, but with the departure of the European Community, we were the only game in town and slowly but surely had already been getting involved. We agreed that we had to involve the Bosnian Serbs in any cease-fire negotiations chaired by the UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Therefore, Colonel, we didn't ask you to recognise our republic, Republika Srpska, but to respect the Serb side without which there could be no negotiations and which was part of the legitimate system, a third of the legitimate system in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So why was that so difficult to do? Why was it so difficult to accept that, for the European Commission to accept that? I mean, the European Community to accept that.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no issue here about the European Community, not accepting the Bosnian Serbs as one of the legitimate ethnic groupings in Bosnia. If you're asking me why the Bosnian Serbs weren't invited to negotiations which I was involved in, I can give you answer to that. So I'm not too sure what your question is. There's never been any doubt that the Bosnian Serbs were part of the entity there. No one is disputing that. The other thing I'll tell you is General Lewis Mackenzie was a United Nations military commander, in command of a considerable amount of troops and represented the United Nations. I did not represent the United Nations. I didn't represent the European Community. I represented the International Peace Conference on the former Yugoslavia, and it is, you know, General MacKenzie can be cross-examined himself. His views of it may be different to mine and are in many instance, but I would just remind you that even though we were all trying to do the same thing, General MacKenzie was a United Nations military officer. I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that document. May I tender it into evidence now, please, the book, although we'll come back to the book in due course a number of times, I believe. Well, I can tender it later on if need be. May we have 1D01270. Just to round off this topic. And you'll see there a letter there General Kukanjac to Alija Izetbegovic, written on the 19th of April. You were there at the time. And General Kukanjac is writing to Izetbegovic -- I think we have the translation of that too. Yes, we do. I'm going to read it out in Serbian, just some of the more pertinent portions: "Mr. President, in the course of the night of the April 17th through the 18th, 1992, your Green Berets carried out an attack on part of a factory in Vogosca, Pretis, the mortar and artillery ammunition production, you are aware of the results of the attack. "In the course of the night of the 18th of April through to the 19th, 1992, in Konjic, at 2000 hours on the 18th of April everything was blocked. All telephones of the PTT were turned off to military facilities. The Green Berets occupied the military equipment factory of Igman." And then lower down says: "Mr. President, a cease of all attacks on military facilities," and under C, "order the deblocking of military facilities Ljuta and Celebic." And on the next page -- we can stay there with the English page, it's on that same page in English or perhaps not, perhaps not. It says, "Mr. President --" What? Yes, we stay there with the English: "Do not forget that we have signed a peace agreement -- we signed a peace agreement on the 12th of April, 1992, and at that very same day your command to attack or where you declare war on the JNA was released and directed of course at Serbs and other innocent citizens." And the last paragraph: "Analyse all this and state publicly that you want war. If you don't want war then demonstrate it through your actions." Now, all this was happening when you were Lord Carrington's envoy to the peace conference. Should you have known about this, and are they circumstances under which the conference was to take place and that those circumstances and the situation affected the conference itself and it's outcome? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I've seen this document. I'm not aware that it was sent by anybody. I wasn't aware of its content, and therefore I can't comment on it. I can only say on the 18th of April that was the day that the television was mortar bombed by Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know all that, but you don't know all that the Muslim forces did; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not totally aware of what anybody did at this stage. I mean, you have to appreciate this city was under siege. It is bound to have allegations flying all over the place, and of course we need to get the background to them. But most of the concern for the international community was what was happening to the city from outside the city to wit the mortaring and shelling of the city from outside. That was the main concern. I find it -- I find it very difficult to understand why there are so many allegations against Muslims carrying out all these actions in the city that was basically under siege, where freedom of movement was denied, where we were spending a lot of time in bunkers. So I find these -- these documents surprising to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, do you know who was doing the shelling? Did you know that it was the HOS and its artillery who were present in Sarajevo? Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
