utterances.text: I was aware that there were elements inside the city that were attempting to defend the city and that there were elements inside the city that were fighting for territory. Yes, I'm aware of that. I don't know the exact details of it, but the predominantly -- the predominant action that was taking place around that period was the shelling of the city and different parts of the city from weapons that were placed on the hills surrounding the city of Sarajevo. That's why most of us were taking shelter in bunkers in the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know who was on the hillsides around Sarajevo? Did you know who held which position?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know, but we were -- we were very well aware of the fact that it was predominantly Bosnian Serbs, because they had already established a Bosnian Serb Army. All of the tanks, heavy artillery, mortars were taken up. I've seen evidence of that in a document that I think has already been placed here from a meeting of the Republika Srpska's committee when it talked about all of the weapons they'd already taken. So I think it is beyond dispute or doubt but that the vast and overwhelming bulk of the armaments at that time were belonging and controlled by the Bosnian Serbs and they were directing this against the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We must be precise, lieutenant [as interpreted], sir, so please don't get angry with me. But can you tell me did the Bosnian Serbs have their own army up until the 12th of May, until the time that you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it's well known that the decision on forming the army was adopted on the 12th of May at the Assembly session in Banja Luka and that the Serbian Army -- the Bosnian Serb Army came into being on the 20th of May, because on the 19th of May the JNA withdrew from Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA withdrew from Bosnia on that date. I agree with that. But you don't create an army overnight, Mr. Karadzic. We saw evidence of massive convoys of armaments and tanks going up the road to Pale to the Republika Srpska headquarters. I've already mentioned that I went up there on the 1st of May with Mrs. Plavsic. I attempted to get up the day before that but the roads were blocked with so many tanks and artillery pieces heading up to Pale that were taken over by from the Bosnian Serbs from the JNA who, at that stage, were anxious to withdraw from the territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose tanks with those? Were they JNA tanks and when did the Serbs -- the Bosnian Serbs take them over from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that they were taken over at the time I saw them going up to Pale. And I also recall that when you were coming to a meeting yourself at Ilidza that you came in one of these tanks yourself with the JNA protection. So I don't know exactly. I know when the decision -- I know when the announcement was made on the creation of the Bosnian Serb Army, but there was a huge amount of military movement before that. One of the missions given to the ECMM was to monitor the movement of convoys of the JNA that were withdrawing from the territory of Croatia. That was one of the tasks I was given when I was head of the mission and we did this and we watched the movement of many convoys of the JNA coming through Bosnia and heading on to other territories such as Serbia. However, a considerable amount of those convoys were, to our mind, coming under the immediate control of the Bosnian Serbs who very quickly established a Bosnian Serb Army, because the arrangement was that anybody who was from the territory of Bosnia that was a member of the JNA, they could remain in Bosnia. Most of these were Serbs and not alone did they remain, but they took with them their equipment and tanks, et cetera. So it was beyond dispute as what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's a lot that is disputable. Where did General Delic come from, from which army?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, where did Hajrulahovic come from who you did meet? Where did the command cadre of the Muslim army come from, and where did they get their initial weaponry? I'm not talking about second or third deliveries of weapons which arrived from Iran, but anyway, where did they get the weapons from in the first place? And do you agree that the JNA was the mother of all the armies in the republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accepted that the JNA represented all of the republics of the former Yugoslavia, and I do accept that there were elements of Bosnian Serbs -- or Bosnian Muslims and Croats who had access to weapons. What I'm saying here is the overwhelming bulk of the withdraw army from Croatia and its equipment was given to the Bosnian Serbs. I'm not denying for a moment that some of those members of the JNA who were Bosnian Muslims became part of the territorial army. I'm not saying that. What I am saying is that the overwhelming bulk of the retreating -- not of the retreating, but of the JNA that were being monitored leaving Croatia by agreement, a lot of those who were Bosnians, that were Bosnian Serbs, became part of the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put something to you, Colonel, sir. Croats and Muslims, for a long period of time were gradually leaving the JNA, so the JNA predominantly became a Serb army. The Serbs were not leaving the JNA until the very end, so that the Serbs inherited these things at once while the Muslims and the Croats did that, gradually seizing the weapons from the JNA. So the JNA is the mother of all the republican armies which were being created from the police forces and the Territorial Defence units of those republics, as well as the JNA units that were leaving the JNA. Croats and Muslims were leaving the army gradually and the Serbs did not. So that is why you have the impression that the Serbs inherited the JNA. But it's only because they did not leave the army until the very end. Would you agree that all the armies were actually created out of the JNA except the Croats and the Muslims were leaving the army gradually and the Serbs did not do that until the very end? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only repeat what I've said earlier, that it was known that 80 per cent -- approximately 80 per cent of the JNA army that went into Bosnia were Bosnian, and most of those were Bosnian Serbs. And so overnight you had a -- nearly overnight you had an easy transition from JNA units become Bosnian Serb units. It would have applied to Croats and Muslims on a much smaller scale. The second reason why the Bosnian Serbs were armed was because President Izetbegovic had declared a state of neutrality and therefore directed that for the federal JNA call-up of reservists that those who were Muslims and Croats would not have to obey that, and they didn't. Therefore, most of the people who obeyed the call for mobilisation were Bosnian Serbs, and they were issued with weapons when they were mobilised, and those weapons they were allowed to retain when they were demobilised. So you had a gradual arming of Bosnian Serbs, and this was not done to any great extent to the Bosnian Muslims. So it was natural that they were going to have access to weapons. And it was a cause of concern to the monitor mission. We had reports coming in of concern being expressed by various opstina that Bosnian Serbs were being gradually armed because they were obeying the call for mobilisation. President Izetbegovic said that it wasn't, in his view, legal and therefore many Bosnian Muslims did not obey the call-up for mobilisation. So that would be another factor in the gradual arming of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you that during our interview we talked about it. I asked you whether you few about the Tito's -- about Tito's doctrine of an armed peoples, about the Law on All Peoples Defence and Social Protection, and that a long time before the war reservists were allowed to take weapons and their uniforms and equipment home. This was long before the war began. So do you remember that we discussed all these questions?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was something that was generally known. Colonel, sir, do you know when the Muslim side began to create it's own armed forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of as to when that happened. I don't -- I knew, of course, that the president was Alija Izetbegovic, and that therefore as president and president of the Presidency that he had a certain amount of influence, but I had concerns because I was called into the Presidency to be told of the concerns of the Presidency at one, the gradual arming of the Bosnian Serbs, and two, that there were munitions coming into the territory of Bosnia that were not officially labelled, and they were coming in in trucks. And I had an incident where the prime minister at the time at Peladin [phoen] asked me to meet with the JNA to find out a reason as to why these weapons were coming in to the JNA. I'm not saying they went to the Bosnian Serbs. At that time they went to the JNA. So these were issues that were being discussed earlier on in the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you accept that the JNA could, just like any other army, engage other transport vehicles to transfer its equipment somewhere else? That was the case, and the army did confirm that it was theirs. Do you agree that any army in the world can engage another company to transport -- or for transport services on its behalf?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have experience of that from my country. We use military equipment for the transfer of military goods. I was concerned at that time because the manifest -- the manifest that was with that convoy I was told - I don't have evidence of this but I was informed by the prime minister - that the manifest of that convoy of four civilian trucks had no mention of rocket launchers that were subsequently found on those trucks and that was what created concern. And I can also say on record here that it was my recommendation to the prime minister that the weapons be released to the JNA and that it would be of advantage to the Presidency if it began to open dialogue with the JNA as an army. Up to that time this wasn't being done. So at my suggestion there was some contact done officially with the JNA, something which wasn't done before I met the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, sir, I'm going to put some facts to you and you can just say whether you agree with the possibility, rule it out or not. Mr. Izetbegovic, in February, two months after the first democratic power was established in Bosnia and Herzegovina, formed a secret committee for the protection of Muslims even though by the very nature of his function he was the president of the council for defence of all the three peoples. Do you allow for this fact to be true or do you disagree that that was the time when this secret commission for the defence of Muslim was formed, for the defence of Muslims? This was in February 1991.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. I've absolutely no -- no idea on that. I didn't go to Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Thank you. And along that line do you know that on the 31st of March, 1991, a decision was adopted on the formation of the Patriotic League as the secret army of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that. Again I didn't go to Bosnia until October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to put this to you: Do you know that this Patriotic League was formed on the 30th of April and that from that time on all the Muslim fighter's date of service began to be recorded, the date of service for all Muslim fighters began on the 30th of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in 103 municipalities, with the exception of only six Croat municipalities, so 103 municipalities where Serbs and Muslims lived together, brigades were formed in -- of the Patriotic Leagues in all of them. So a secret army was being formed in all of these municipalities where Serbs and Muslims were living together?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that already at that time arming began and they were receiving weapons from all over and that when the conflict began they received weapons from Iran with the knowledge of the United States continuously through Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you, Colonel, sir, that the new year, 1992, we awaited with 103.000 of our armed Muslims belonging to the Patriotic League, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that I'd be very, very surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what would you say if I were to tell you that on the 27th of June, 1991, President Kucan, President Tudjman, and the presiding President of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina Alija Izetbegovic, made a secret alliance against Yugoslavia and the JNA? This was a military alliance intended to wage war against Yugoslavia and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very reluctant to interrupt, and you probably have already seen that I do not object much, but the witness is -- has said he has no knowledge, and he came in 19 -- he came at October 1991. So these questions do not lead anywhere, and I just wonder when this will be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some of the questions were related to 1992, after he arrived, and then I understood him to be putting his case. So let's be brief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to state the following: The distinguished colonel, Mr. Doyle, whom we always respected and still do, arrived and faced a situation that he did not know much about, and I'm convinced that Colonel Doyle would have viewed matters differently had he known of the secret alliance, war alliance, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not make your speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just explaining why I consider this to be relevant. The colonel did not know then what he knows now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have the opportunity to explain to the Chamber as to the credibility or the relevance of the evidence later on. This is the time for you to put your question instead of making speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that you agreed when we had our interview that you did not know who Dr. Karadzic controlled -- or, rather, which formations, which units at that time, and that your idea about Karadzic controlling something is based on the fact that Karadzic had an armed escort; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have taken it that as the leader of the Bosnian Serbs you would have had responsibility for all elements of Bosnian Serbs under your control, and that, in my view, would have included military. That is the normal. When one is a leader, one accepts responsibility for what his subordinates do or failed to do. Therefore I would have assumed and it would have been the same for the Bosnian Muslims under President Izetbegovic, that the political leaders who control these people, they're the ones who accept -- who should take responsibility. So it's in that light that I would have understood you to be the undisputed leader of the Bosnian Serbs. I mean, I -- I'm certainly willing to state that there would always be elements that are not under central control, some radicals, but by and large it is the norm for political masters to control military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we're talking here about something that happened up -- up to the 12th of May, and you agreed and said that you don't know that I controlled certain formations up until the 12th of May. So we're not talking about the situation after the 20th of May when the Army of Republika Srpska existed but while you were there. You agreed that while you were there, you had no knowledge of and were not aware of me controlling any formations. But you've said in your statement that you saw that I had an armed escort. Now, did you agree when we met that that armed escort was assigned to us by the ministry -- or, rather, the police and that they were employees of the regular police force?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had the meeting and you put that to me, I accepted what you said. Yes, I accept that. I'm not in a position of saying when exactly I can recall whether any of these suddenly became armed Bosnian Serbs, because at that time they were many armed forces who were in uniform and out of uniform and it was very difficult to get a handle on exactly who was what, but when I saw you on occasions that you had an escort, some of them did not appear to me to be in uniform so I wasn't too sure who they were. So I accept when you say they were given to you by the police. I have no reason to disbelieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you know, based on this document -- well, the second page in Serbian -- or, rather, from this letter by General Kukanjac to Alija Izetbegovic, don't forget that we reached an agreement on a truce on the 12th of April, and that afterwards they issued a directive declaring war on the JNA? Did you know about this cease-fire, the truce? You said previously, I believe, that you knew of this 12th of April cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in -- at that stage I had returned to Sarajevo on the 10th of April, and I was involved -- or I was witness to the negotiations that were going on in Ilidza in order to get that cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that on that very same day, Hasan Efendic sent a secret directive for war against all JNA facilities, to block roads, cut off electricity and water and everything that happened to the JNA in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we published that, and we sent it out to the mediators in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to tender this letter by General Kukanjac to Mr. Izetbegovic into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has actually said that he cannot confirm anything in this letter, and he cannot deal with the letter, and therefore the position is actually as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We agree. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he did confirm it, Your Excellency. He said that he took part, that he was a peace broker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He couldn't comment on it. We do not admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D0178 is the document I'd like called up on e-court next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, let me ask you, Colonel, whether you knew of attacks by the Muslim army against Nedzarici and the JNA installations, weapons theft and so on?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had been informed that there were some attacks by Muslim elements against some of the JNA installations with a view to attempting to get weapons, but I had no written report of it and I wasn't in a position of verifying that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we have a document which refers to your interview to "Vecernje Novosti" on the 12th of May, 1992, and this is what it says: "Lord Carrington's personal envoy gave a statement saying that he was going home." And there's a better variant: "... saying that he is returning home tired and exhausted from meeting with hundreds of different people during --" et cetera. Now, at the bottom it says: "Colonel Doyle stressed that he does -- that an attack on the JNA ammunition storage depot near Nedzarici is inconceivable to him by which the Rump Presidency once again violated the agreement and word they had given. If we agree upon something and if we confirm all the details," this is a quotation, "he says, 'Completely unbelievable that that which was agreed on is not respected,' said Doyle. I believe that in Sarajevo at the time nobody has complete control of the situation, that the many armed forces are outside of any kind of control. That is perhaps the reason for the attack, which unfortunately there were once again dead and wounded men." Do you remember giving that interview?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit I don't -- I don't actually remember. I gave -- I gave many interviews, but I actually don't remember this one. Now, when this is dated the 12th of May, on the 12th of May I was up at 5.00 a.m. because I had to go to Lukavica because I was told that I was being evacuated by aircraft to Belgrade. So I presume the -- the interview didn't take place on the 12th of May. Maybe the paper was issued on the 12th of May, but I certainly don't recall that specific interview, no. If I had time to analyse the document, I could give a view on it, but I'm just -- I'm -- I'm -- it -- it's coming as a surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, yes, that's correct. These -- the paper was published on the 12th of May. So I assume that you made the statement at least one day prior to that if not more. But let's see what it says in reference to the 3rd of May, when the military column was massacred. Mr. Doyle had this to say: "Even with the passage of the military convoy, everything was arranged beforehand and that crime should not have happened, although I must say that during the evacuation of the army and command of other military regions there were military mistakes being made; namely prior to the decision to move, I had forewarned General Milutin Kukanjac that a column of 25 vehicles was far too large and I had told General MacKenzie that it was far too late to start moving." Do you remember saying that and that position of yours?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this now, Your Excellency. May it be received?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted as.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D216, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now may we have called up again 1D1291, which is General MacKenzie's book, and it's page 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the attack on the column in your interview, the events of the 3rd of May, we're now just going to glance at this passage where your name is mentioned. I'm going to read it out in English: "[In English] By the 3rd, definitely it was the worst day in my life begins my diary for this date. Around midmorning, Bosnian vice-president Ejup Ganic came to my office and met with me and Colm Doyle of the EC. Ganic explained that President Izetbegovic, on his return from Lisbon, had been kidnapped at the Sarajevo airport; he was being detained by the JNA at their Lukavica camp, just east of the runway. Ganic said he was not a strong leader and needed his president back in ordered to control the radical officers within the Bosnian Territorial Defence forces, who were rapidly getting out of control. Territorial Defence forces had General Kukanjac's headquarters under siege in the eastern part of city; Ganic feared that if they attacked the general's barracks, the JNA would retaliate by levelling Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Do you remember Ganic's arrival in General MacKenzie's office?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know how long the siege of the 2nd Military District lasted, command and headquarters?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure, but I knew that the military headquarters was surrounded by -- by Bosnian Muslims, that I can verify. And when General MacKenzie said to me the United Nations did not have a mandate to work in Bosnia, he asked if I would chair the negotiations to initiate the -- to try to secure the release of the president against General Kukanjac, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I tell you that it was weeks before and that the headquarters was under siege by the Green Berets weeks before this incident, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I actually don't know, so I've no reason not to accept it, but it -- it gave -- it gave me ammunition to do a deal, to swap the president for the general, and that's what I set about to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure you'll remember that before that an agreement was reached about the way in which the JNA would be withdrawing and that the government guaranteed it. We have the document here. I think the Prosecution presented it. Do you remember that such a document did exist, that the Muslim part of the authorities guaranteed security during the withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact detail of that, but what I can say is that I was very, very concerned when we had what I thought an agreement that we would swap the presidential party for General Kukanjac, and an officer of colonel rank who was in the room decided that the ante, as they say, would be put up. And instead of Kukanjac getting out he wanted the entire military headquarters. Now as a military officer, the same for General MacKenzie, we knew that to withdraw a full military force from a sieged barracks was something that was very dangerous and we were anxious that the information would be given to the Bosnian Muslims. We told the president that we felt this was not a viable option, that withdrawing all of these troops with all of their equipment would not be accepted by the Muslims who were surrounding the -- the headquarters, but this colonel was extremely abusive to me, and he tried to thwart my efforts to get the president out. So what I'm saying in essence is that yes, we were aware that the military headquarters was surrounded by armed Bosnian Muslims, and we were very concerned that even though the president said he could guarantee the security of the convoy, neither General MacKenzie nor my myself believed that this could actually take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And we see: "[In English] Ganic was extremely shaken by this news. He almost lost control. Colm and I decided to go to the JNA camp at Lukavica to find out what was happening." [Interpretation] May we turn to the next page, please. Do you agree with this? Yes, you do? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry? Do --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that passage I read out correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now on the next page: "[In English] The president was on the phone talking to General Kukanjac and seemed to be in pretty good spirits." [Interpretation] Do you confirm that too?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that because for the first two hours we were in Lukavica I was not in with the president. I stayed outside. And General MacKenzie was dealing with the president, and he came out to let me know that the deal we had originally negotiated had now fallen through because there was a conversation between the president, I understand, and General Kukanjac which I wasn't privy to. And then I was told this colonel came to me and said that -- that there was going to be a difficulty because the deal we had arranged at the headquarters of the UN in the city was now negated, and I was getting very frustrated and very annoyed. I was also concerned that if this drew on much longer that darkness would fall, and trying to move a convoy in darkness would be very serious. So I gave my views, but the president said, I will guarantee the security of the convoy. And then the -- the colonel changed his mind and -- because he didn't want to release the other members of the Presidency. He said to me, You've just negotiated the release of the president, not his daughter or a security officer or another member of the Presidency. So in trying to get this problem solved, I was certainly held as a hostage myself, or I was held back as collateral. So what happened from the time the convoy left Lukavica barracks with the president inside to the time that the president got to the Presidency I have no idea. I certainly know what happened from looking at it in television and getting reports, but I was not witness to the operation. I do know and accept that the convoy was attacked and that approximately five or six members of the JNA were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm afraid that there's more to that, but what you have just said more or less is also written in this book by General MacKenzie about how you were against such a large evacuation and that Izetbegovic accepted responsibility. I would now like us to look at the next one, two, three, four pages ahead, please. On this page we can see: "[In English] At that moment we heard the claxon horn on the approaching emergency vehicle. It was a JNA ambulance. The driver was frantically sowing [phoen] on the steering wheel trying to avoid hitting anyone. His task was made all of the more difficult to JNA colonel collapsed on his right shoulder and missing half his face. The colonel was obviously dead or about to die." [Interpretation] A bit lower: "[In English] It seemed that wherever we were the killing stopped. The stealing of equipment was still going on but at least people weren't being executed." [Interpretation] General MacKenzie is describing, because he was there at the scene, he believes that more people were killed than what you described and now there are proceedings being conduced. Ganic has been arrested in London as one of those responsible for what happened. Now can we go to the next page, please. It's a pity that you were not at the scene. Did General MacKenzie inform you about what happened?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember an exact conversation with him. I -- I was very concerned about my own safety when I was held at Lukavica because I was threatened with a pistol. So I really had my own concerns about my own future. But really I wasn't witness to -- as soon as the president left Lukavica, I was out of it, so I had no detailed knowledge of what happened after that, nor was I witness to it. So I really can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page, 170, we have to look at the page -- the bottom part of the page: "At this point General Kukanjac started pacing back and forth [In English] Across the street, shouting that he was missing at least 200 soldiers as he had to go back for them." [No interpretation]: "[In English] I told him that if he did so, he would be killed for sure." [No interpretation]: "[In English] I ordered him back into Steve's vehicle. Reluctantly he obeyed it, his face expressing the agony of someone who cared for his soldiers." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the Serbs expected that the presence of international forces would make the evacuation safe and that they had sufficient reason to be angry because of this massacre? Regardless of whether they were right or not, did the Serbs have the feeling that they could rely on the presence of international forces and on the word of the president, President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can say here is that when the president said that he would -- that he would guarantee the safety of the convoy we disagreed with him and we told him he wasn't in a position to guarantee the safety of the convoy. And as military officers, we would not have been happy with this arrangement. However, he was the president of the country. He had assured us he would guarantee the security of the convoy. It was a very dangerous situation. This military barracks was surrounded, and as we know, we had talked about approximately 27 trucks, but it was a lot more than 27 trucks that left that military headquarters. This is what we had suspected. So I have no doubt that -- I have no reason to disagree with anything that is pointed out here by General MacKenzie because he was at the screen and I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you were there on the 6th of May when Mr. Ludwig was there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Goulding, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the eighth page after this one, please. On the 5th of May, Marrack Goulding, the UN under-secretary for special political affairs, was in Pale. Later, he was escorted by General MacKenzie, and then it says: "[In English] After our initial escort party was held up by fighting in the east of Sarajevo, General Nambiar insisted that he lead the next attempt." [Interpretation] And then lower it says: "[In English] On the 6th of May I spent a full day with Mr. Goulding, briefing him all morning. In the afternoon, we went on a tour of the city with President Izetbegovic and came under modest fire in the middle of the Muslim old city. There were very strong indications that it was an orchestrated show for the accompanying media intended to put the Serbs in a bad light." [Interpretation] Were you aware of these moves that were supposed to blacken the Serbs' reputation?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, because on the 5th of May I was chairing a cease-fire negotiation at the PTT building as a consequence or a follow-up to the release of the president. So all that day, and in fact, from that day to the day that I was evacuated, I don't believe I left the PTT building at all. My total focus no was on, one, getting a cease-fire as a consequence of the -- securing the release of the president, and second, on negotiations to effect the total withdraw of the JNA army from Bosnia. So what was going on in the city, what was going in the United Nations, I wasn't aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at the following paragraph: "I also went at my request --" Mr. Goulding is giving his assessment of what happened with the cold-blooded killings of the soldiers and the commanders by the Bosnian Territorial Defence, and General MacKenzie says in the following paragraph: "[In English] Later when I had left Sarajevo for good I was surprised to see just how little media covered Goulding's strong statement as received around the world. I couldn't help thinking that if the JNA had ambushed the Territorial Defence forces instead of the other way around, it would have been front-page news." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the world media was partial and that the Serbs had a more difficult time of it in the world media?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I mean, the world's media felt that this was a conflict started by Milosevic, and there was a certain amount of sympathy to the Bosnian Muslims. So in the eyes of the world, yes, I would say that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to show in the course of these proceedings that it was the other way around.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender these sections of General MacKenzie's book, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the convoy incident description, that's chapter 17, I agree. No opposition here. In relation to the chapter 18, it's basically General MacKenzie's viewpoints. However, as it was at least addressed by Colonel Doyle in one aspect, I also agree to have this chapter 18 admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He didn't confirm anything about -- on page 182 or page 22 of the e-court in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But given it's all 23 pages, shall we admit it in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so. Would I say so, although he wasn't part in -- of the events at some stage, but at least it's sort of related, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D217, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm noting the time. We will have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just in relation to one document, we have clarified the situation in relation to the Defence Exhibit 1D01210. The text provided is consistent with the actual minutes of the 56th session of the Presidency, which were disclosed to the Defence, and we are just providing the details where they can find it, but unfortunately we also do not have a translation. So the full translation is still outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we're talking about D214, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's the minutes and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If these are the minutes from the 56th session of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then it's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. Let's move on. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, Colonel, you said you'd agreed that you had attended the 24th of January meeting of the Bosnian Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you also agreed that I proposed that regionalisation be undertaken first so the Serbs could go to the referendum and that Muhamed Cengic proposed that the government be given a fortnight to carry out the regionalisation and that proposal was accepted by me; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember sitting in the Assembly for the duration of that debate, but you'll have to accept that I -- can I had an interpreter with me, so I didn't get, you know, the full translations of everything that was said. So -- so I was there and I understood what generally the debate was about, but the exact details I wouldn't be competent, I think, to -- to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. I accepted Muhamed Cengic's proposal, and we'll call up that document, a document that bears it out, if need be, and I went up to the microphone together with him, and for two and a half hours people thought that an agreement had been reached and the government would carry out regionalisation within a fortnight and that the Serbs would go to the referendum regardless of how they would be voting, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say I remember the specifics. I was tasked by the headquarters of the monitor mission to attend the referendum debate to give them the result of what the debate was, not necessarily all of the content of it. So the report that I made out was -- was pretty general in terms, but not the exact details, because it went on for so long. It went on throughout the entire night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have D87 called up next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To refresh our memories, Colonel, because it appeared that we had saved Bosnia. So I set great store by that. This was one such situation when we thought we might have saved Bosnia. And later on there was, of course, the conference, the Cutileiro conference during your stay in Bosnia. But anyway, may we have called up 1D0087 next, please. It's an exhibit. And may we have page 103 of this document displayed, please. It's a meeting of the joint Assembly, the tape recording of it. The date is the 24th of January, 1992, and may we turn to page 103, please. Let's see what Mr. Cengic says here, Muhamed Cengic, and I'm reading the Serbian version: "Ladies and gentlemen, I would like to inform you and something to you. The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we are seeing Mr. Cengic's words here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now we have it. Thank you. At the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I would like to inform you and suggest something. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina received the order, made its decision to establish -- to carry out the regionalisation, a new regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think the Serbian democratic party as well as the Party of Democratic Action, the Croatian Democratic Union, need to make their own requests on this regionalisation, what should be done, and I think that it would be useful if this regionalisation were to be carried out. It's the task of the government too. And we should schedule a referendum date and to set the dead-line for both the referendum and the establishment of regions. There will be no referendum before the plan for the regionalisation is presented. I think that that would be a good solution and that it would satisfy all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because it's useless for us to talk about what all the Serbs want, to live in all -- in one state or the Muslims, or anybody else, but we have to start talking and discussing the matter amongst ourselves. Therefore, the proposal that I have offered up now, and Mr. Karadzic agrees with it, I think is a good one, an acceptable one, and I'd like to hear your views on the matter." Now, may we turn to the next portion to see what Karadzic says. Right down at the bottom of the page. Can we scroll down there. Next page, in fact -- yes, that's right. Radovan Karadzic. I'll read it in English. I don't see it in Serbian: "[In English] You will forgive me because my voice is not the best. Just when we think we agreed, we distort --" [Interpretation] I see. I found that now: "[In English] We actually change the entire essence. It is clear that B and H cannot prevent or avoid the changes that are going on around it. It cannot. Those changes request that new factual state is sanctioned and that the legality and new legal state is achieved. In that sense, new referendum would be acceptable to the --" [Interpretation] Next page, please: "[In English] ... Serbian people provided that a new democratic transformation of B and H into a new state which all three sovereign nations would accept, would be carried out prior to that. Therefore, I believe that for a new state, all three people would participate in the national and collective civil referendum. Nothing is possible in B and H without the consensus of three peoples. I have to present to you what I would mean -- what it would mean if we do not do this way. If we do not do this way, we would create the conditions for the independent state to be announced without our consent. Because according to the unconstitutional law and -- the law that is not in accordance with the constitution, it is said that 51 per cent of the votes is needed for the referendum to be recognised. The existing law is unconstitutional, and it is not adjusted to the constitution because it is written in the constitution that there should be 66.6 per cent of the votes for the referendum to be recognised. For any changes of the situation according to the new constitution, we need 66.6 of the votes and Serbs and Croats do not have 66 per cent votes together, and they will participate less and less in the general population of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, it -- if we hold a referendum before the transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbs and Croats are imprisoned, locked in their internationally recognised borders that no one can -- ever can change. They are in total power of the host and the boss of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say, those who are majority now and who will be outnumbered," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] So you can see, Colonel, that the Muslims managed to have the constitution changed with a 51 per cent of the votes at the referendum, which is completely or was completely unconstitutional, and there is no constitution in the world which can be amended if there's only 51 per cent votes in the -- on the referendum and in the Assembly. So do you see that we were tricked and forced to do something that was unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think to clarify this point, Your Honour, I would just like to say that at the conclusion of this marathon session of the Assembly, I compiled a report to -- to my headquarters and that report gave a general outline as I understood it to be of what the issues were. I was sufficiently concerned to put in that report the fact that according to the Bosnian Serbs there was a requirement for an agreement to be done by consensus, whereas most of the people in the parliament seem to be going along the line of where they are going to pass a referendum if they had a majority. What that majority was I wasn't aware. But I did put down that maybe this is something that needed to be checked out legally. So as a consequence of that, I sought a meeting with the supreme legal court, or whatever, of Bosnia, and I met with them the following day to find out whether or not the allegations by the Bosnian Serbs that this referendum debate was constitutional, because I'm not a lawyer. And I met with all of these senior Judges of Bosnia, Serb, Croat, and Muslim, and when I put that to them, a female member of the -- of the senior legal branch said, Mr. Doyle, you don't understand. I'm a Serb and this person is a Croat and this person is a Muslim. We can't agree amongst ourselves as to what is constitutional or not because we all follow our own political philosophies. So even having a meeting with the senior legal brains of Bosnia, they could not give me collectively a definitive answer as to whether or not that debate or whether the referendum was to be constitutional or not, and I put that as part of my report which was sent to the headquarters. The exact detail, Dr. Karadzic, that you were bringing up, I simply -- I'm simply not in a position to comment on because this was a debate that went on for hours and hours and hours of legal wranglings in a language I don't understand and at a level which I'm not commensurate with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is already an exhibit, so I don't have to tender it. It's already been admitted. But you saw the development of events. There was a referendum that we did not take part in, but we didn't challenge it either. And then we come to the 3rd of March. Do you remember what happened on the 3rd of March in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar of what happened outside of Sarajevo on the 3rd of March, but only in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, while we still have this document on our screens, do you agree that Lord Carrington's position was also that all three sides should agree, should reach an agreement, on what Bosnia should look like, that there should be no competition between all sides but they should all agree, reach an agreement?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that when I was with Lord Carrington and that question was proposed to him at a press conference at the airport. His view was that as far at the peace conference in Yugoslavia was concerned, any agreement that would be agreed by all sides, no matter what that agreement was, once they agreed that was sufficient for the European Union that the role of the peace conference was to be -- act as a good office for these peoples to come up with a solution that would not include violence. So it wasn't a matter for the peace conference or certainly it wasn't a matter for Lord Carrington to decide what sort of a solution should be -- should be established rather than saying whatever you agree collectively together, three different parties, I'm happy with whatever that is once you agree. So really he was putting the onus back on the parties to try to come up with a solution that might be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 18th an agreement was indeed reached with respect to the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the exact contents of that agreement. I wasn't party to it. But it was brought to my attention, because on the 18th of March I wasn't with Lord Carrington. I was still head of the mission, and I was told that an agreement had almost been reached and as far as I recall that the Muslims reneged or went back on that agreement, but the exact content of the agreement, I wasn't familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all that remained was for the maps to be precisely defined and to resolve the question of a joint army. Everything else was accepted. All right. Perhaps you weren't there, but they gave up on the 25th and already on the 25th and 26th there was bloodshed again of Serbs in Bosanski Brod, Sijekovac, and so on. Did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well let's move on to the 12th straight away and for that may I have 1D01256 displayed, please. And at the time, you were already in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not going to look at anything before the 10th, although there were significant events during that period. May we have the English version displayed as well, please, alongside the Serbian. Do you remember that on that day a truce was signed? And we have the document in which, among other things, the cease-fire said that work on the maps should be accelerated. Do you remember that? I'm referring to the cease-fire. A cease-fire was signed on that day.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will look at the document a little later on, but let's see what the commander of the Green Berets is writing, the Green Berets of Bosnia-Herzegovina. His name was Sead Ahmetovic. The Green Berets staff it says Sarajevo, BH, telegram, strictly confidential. The 12th of April, 1992, is the date, and it says police station, Visegrad. That's who it is addressed to. So that police -- well, it says: "Please convey the message of Murat Sabanovic, the Green Berets' commander for the region of Visegrad and its surroundings, to blow up the Visegrad Dam as soon as possible." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with that. I would say here that one of the most frustrating elements of what we were doing in Bosnia was to try and get cease-fires which were passed with what I would call monotonous regularity, because as soon as they were -- as soon as they were signed, they were broken. So it seemed to be an exercise in futility. This specific incident, no, I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a photocopy of this original document as well, but at that time there was a crisis and on television we have Kukanjac and Izetbegovic and this man Murat Sabanovic, and they entreated him not to blow up the dam, and Izetbegovic entreated him saying, Murat, not for now. Don't do it for the time being. Which means that the opportunity would be there later on. Do you remember there was a live television broadcast where they wanted to convince him not to go ahead? And that was a real crisis. You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the incident but not the detail, but, yes, I remember a lot of discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reliability of this document to me is doubtful. The witness has no details on this. Therefore, I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he remembers some discussion going around in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. Yes. Okay. No objection then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Based upon the Chamber's observation that I just spoke about, we'll admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D218, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have document 1D01108, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01108. We have it in Serbian. I don't know if there is a translation of it. I believe there is. The Prosecution has the document. I don't know what their number is, but I know they do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you what this document is about. First of all, the date is the 20th of April, and it is the premier of the Serbian Republic of -- Republika Srpska, professor Dr. Branko Djeric is issuing an order and saying: "Artillery fire and heavy weapons fire is forbidden from the positions of Serb defence forces on targets in the city of Sarajevo. "2. The use of artillery and heavy weapons on targets in the city of Sarajevo will only be ordered in justified cases by the minister of defence. The implementation of this order shall be seen to," et cetera, et cetera, "and any violations of this order will be strictly punished. The order comes into force immediately." Now, I'd like to tell you, first of all, due to the pressure and the shooting the government declared that the Serb territorials should refrain from shooting in town. Do you agree -- are forbidden from shooting in town. Do you agree that this is something that should be ordered by the supreme commander and the president of the republic and not the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is a document that is -- has come from -- sorry, can I just ask you to repeat the -- the -- this document was issued by?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was issued by the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I want to say that the government had to issue that because at that point in time there was no president of the republic or, rather, the president of the Presidency and there was no Army of Republika Srpska only the Serb territorials who could obey but did not have to. Do you think that it's usual for the prime minister to be issuing an order of this kind?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it probably depends on -- on whether or not it was -- it was obeyed. Around this time there was a considerable amount of shelling of the city of Sarajevo. So if this was issued by the Republika Srpska, it certainly wasn't obeyed, in my estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My point is that the prime minister tried to do what he could without having the tools of enforcing his order. He tried to order the territorials or those who were defending their neighbourhoods to stop firing. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's -- we don't have the -- we don't have the translation of that document here. It's still -- the one I have is still in Serbian, but I'm not too sure why this should have happened when -- when the -- the result was that there was shelling. In other words, the directive wasn't obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, and in fact, we have received a translation. For some reason is -- it's obviously not uploaded in e-court but it exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with that confirmation and then with the anticipation that it will be disclosed to the parties, we'll admit it as evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Exhibit D219.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to have 1D00289, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Colonel, sir, do you remember what my platform was for the resolution of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 22nd of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was quite known to the foreigners, because we had sent it around. We had informed Lord Carrington and Ambassador Cutileiro about it, and it was published in the media. We have it in front of us now. This is a platform indicating what our -- what we were proposing and what we were committing ourselves to. And here it is: "1. An unconditional and immediate cease-fire and compliance with the cease-fire agreement of the 12th of April, 1992." Is this the cease-fire agreement that you were working on?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you: "2. Urgent continuation of the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina and its continuous work until a solution is found. "3. Within the framework of the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina, priority should be given to the drawing of maps of Sarajevo and constituent states. "4. Public commitment by all the parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina that the constituent parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina will not be joined to neighbouring states and that armed forces from outside Bosnia and Herzegovina will not be invited in or accepted in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "5. Public commitment by all the parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina that they will not accept a policy of fait accompli, not even the one arising from the Communist heritage and the territorial advantages gained by means of force will not be recognised. "6. Urgent implementation of a new constitutional agreement along with guarantees of the international community. "7. The opening of the process of demilitarisation and the precise defining of the role of the JNA in the forthcoming period." How does this platform look to you, Colonel, sir. I'm sorry that you didn't know about it before but all of your bosses did know about it. Lord Carrington did and Ambassador Cutileiro did as well. Do you have any remarks to make on this platform and was it a sufficient basis for the continuation of the conference?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at the document it looks very inviting and it looks very attractive, but I'm just wondering why it is that on -- on that same day was the commencement of the first -- first fighting in the city of Sarajevo, and for all of that day I was trying to negotiate a cease-fire so that we could facilitate the arrival of Lord Carrington and the president of the council of ministers of the European Union to Sarajevo airport the following morning. So my focus was that. And it was the following morning, on the 23rd of April, that we were trying to get some progress. So I'm not familiar with the content of this document. Whether this, in actual fact, was to be implemented or not I think is quite another matter. We know that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is not an executive order. This is a commitment by the Serbian side, a proposal of what should be done and our statement that we're not going to accept a policy of fait accompli or territory -- territorial seizure by force and so on. Do you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, avoid making comments. The last comment was unnecessary, unless you put any question to the witness. Bear that in mind. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D220, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at document 1D01109.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you were at -- in Ilidza on the 22nd of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We need 1D01109, please, a different document from this one. This is from the 2nd of May. We will need this one, too, but a bit later. This is not the number, actually, that I asked for. There's something not quite right with the numbers. Can we put this on the ELMO, please? First page first so that we can identify the document, and then -- the number that we did get is 1D01110. [In English] First page and then ... [Interpretation] Up at -- you were in Ilidza when the Muslim forces carried out an attack on Ilidza and this is what is said in the police report: "The attack carried out by Muslim paramilitary formations on the 22nd of April, in the area of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza was a long-prepared and carefully planned one. According to the estimates of the SDA leadership, this area is exceptionally strategically important for the formation of the Islamic state. The leaders of the party approved substantial funds for the procurement of weapons and military equipment and these activities -- and as future financiers many well-off citizens of Ilidza of Muslim nationality participated in it, including the minister of internal affairs of former Bosnia and Herzegovina. All this was aided by some religious officials of the Islamic Community, and in this area that is why four paramilitary formations could have been formed in this area. "According to the information of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a year ago the Party of Democratic Action shipped in weapons to this area, the main supplier was Senaid Memic." And then we can now go to the bottom of the page and then we will move to the next page. We will just need to look at the highlighted parts, please, of the document, the highlighted parts. This is fine. Thank you: "As for Ilidza, the main co-ordinator of all activities about gathering, persuading to join, engaging and arming the population of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity up to a point was Edin Malicevic, the chief of the Ilidza public security service. This document describes how top leadership abused the Ministry of Internal Affairs and at the local affairs where you were, the chief of the public security station in Ilidza, Edin Malicevic was the chief. He first armed the reserve forces of the police of Muslim ethnicity really well and then in the Fuego [phoen] cafe owned by Hamde Vatric together with Hamdo Pasic, a well-known criminal, gathered together mostly younger people of Muslim and Croat ethnicity, enrolled them in the Patriotic League and then he had them at the staff which was close to the cafe Queen and distributed arms to them." Colonel, sir, were you aware that the police was behind these paramilitary formations and was preparing these attacks?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware. I remember the attack in Ilidza on that day, and the defenders were Bosnian Serbs that were being attacked. I don't know who was being attacked. We were under cover because it was very dangerous, and I know that approximately 13 died in that attack. So I was aware that the attack took place and the Serbs were defending, but that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that they were attacked from the Otes neighbourhood as well as from the Sokolovic-Kolonija area and Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would have to say that for most of that day I was in a -- I was in my room or in the hotel. We couldn't leave it. I left -- I left the hotel to do an interview with the BBC, and that was the day that I was -- that was the day I was asked to give my views as to whether or not the meeting the following morning with Pinheiro and Carrington should take place because we wanted to make sure that there was a degree of safety for the visit to take place. So I was concerned about trying to make an assessment of the situation, but I am aware that there was a lot of fighting on, because that was first time I had actually seen fighting in the city of Sarajevo. But the exact direction it was coming from I couldn't say because we were in a location very close to the people who were defending.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to press on with this document any more as it's clear that you did see with your own eyes the attack on the Serbian part of Ilidza and the defence of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we tender this document for identification first, please, because I'm not sure if we have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in principle, yes, but marked for identification because we don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the exact 65 ter number is 1109, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 1109, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D221, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D01258.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting I would like to inform you, Colonel, that this is a directive of the TO staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 23rd of April, 1994. As you know, at that point in time, efforts were continuing to establish a cease-fire on the 12th of April, and this is an endeavour in which you and Ambassador Cutileiro participated. This is a new directive by Hasan Efendic on the defence of the sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do we have that? Unfortunately, we don't have a translation for this either, but I would just like to draw your attention to the first part under number 1 which talks about enemy forces. This is the Territorial Defence of the Serbian autonomous region and the Serbian Army, which is also considered to be an enemy on the 23rd of April, and then in paragraph marked with a number 4 it says: "I have decided immediately to carry out the mobilisation of the entire composition of the TO of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, speedily carry on with the formation of combat units in all municipalities which are to be placed under the Joint Command of municipal, district, and the staff of the TO of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina command, and then -- and forcefully carry out actions to break the assault force of the enemy." Can we please look at the following page: "Immediately carry out the occupation of ammunition depots and block the barracks, occupy them and capture members of the Yugoslav Army on the territory of the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then under 5 it says: "District Staffs of the Territorial Defence form TO units, volunteer units, the Patriotic League of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, TO units, and other patriotic forces in the territory of the municipality all to be under the Joint Command and insignia as decreed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then it says: "While forming the combat disposition of the main force for carrying out active combat and also have auxiliary forces." And then we have on the following page number 7: "To establish a system of command immediately at the level of units, the Municipal Staff, the district staff, republic staff," and so on. The rest is unimportant. "While negotiations are underway for a cease-fire following efforts from the European Community, preparations are being accelerated for carrying on the war while the first is going on. " So did anybody inform you about these activities of Hasan Efendic -- or, rather, the Muslim command in this direction?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not bought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Should it have been brought to your attention? Mediators?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 23rd of April, I was facilitating the arrival of -- of Joao Pinheiro and Peter Carrington to Sarajevo, and all of that day we were involved in negotiations for a cease-fire with all the political parties. You were there yourself, Mr. Karadzic, you will recall, and my task then was to get the leaders back to the airport to actually sign the document, and that in itself was a big, big challenge. So my total focus was on implementing to get the signatures done. We know that a lot of the cease-fires were broken. Who broke them, I have no idea. And there were counter-claims from all sides, but I'm for the familiar with this document. Should it have been brought to my attention? I simply don't know. That's all I can really say on it. I don't have a comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should be marked for identification. At the moment I'm actually not able to say whether this document relates to the evidence of the witness because I can't really read it, and the passages that were read into the record, they seem to be also not adopted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you make a decision, Your Honours, may I inform you that this is a secret document, and after this document there's a public document which is an order from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina through the police that the decision be made for the withdraw of the JNA units and an order about how the JNA should be treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, and when the translation is done, the Chamber will assess its relevance and then decide its admissibility then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D222.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. A Prosecution document, 65 ter 01040. Is that an exhibit? Has that been admitted as an amalgamated document? 65 ter 01040. I think we have it in English. That's the platform. Yes, that's right. And here's this platform in a collection of documents where the Prosecution is conveying some SRNA agency reports. It's dated the 22nd of April -- well, it's a platform of the 22nd of April, published on the 23rd of April. May we see the portion that starts "The truth about the fight on Ilidza," and so on. The bottom of the page in English, please. Thank you. And this is what SRNA reported: "[In English] SRNA is authorised to give an announcement that came from the Serbian police properly or Serbian Republic of Bosnia on 22nd April 1992. Due to the great number of false information which are consciously emitted on the principles of the psychological propagandistic war over the radio and television of Sarajevo, press centre of Serbian Republic of B and H, placed in Ilidza, in the centre of war action brings about following facts: This morning attack was started by the Muslim formations from Sokolovic colony. The members of these units occupied the restaurant Topola and institute of rehabilitation from where they fired from their snipers -- snipers and during that time wounded several members of Serbian police and Territorial Defence of Ilidza. On the Serbian side there were killed people, but their number and identity could be determined only after the possibility of being taken out from the fire zone," and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, that, then, is what confirms what you have just told us; right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes, but again the detail, where it was exactly coming from, where the firing was coming from, I just can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D54 next, please. Is this document -- has this document been admitted, the one we just displayed? Is it admitted -- or, rather, is it an exhibit? Is it an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Exhibit D223.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the Prosecution number. I thought the Prosecution had tendered it, but if not, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We now see that this is a document from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which on the 27th of April, 1992, issued a decision on the withdrawal of JNA units from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and under number 3 down there it says: "Members of the JNA who do not wish to place themselves at the disposal of the state organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for any reason shall be required to leave the territory of the republic of BH in a direction of their choice in organised fashion escorted by organs of the Ministry of the Interior of BH and under the supervision of the European Community observers." May we turn to the next page, please. In English it says: "The state organs of Bis will ensure the unimpeded withdrawal of JNA units." And then under number 5, it says: "The units and institutions to which weapons technical equipment and materiel of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been entrusted for storage are required to hand over these weapons and equipment to their owners, namely the authorised organs of the Territorial Defence of BH."
